questions.title: Explain a sampling procedure

extraPoints.text: Read three-digit groups, reject 000 and 181–999, and ignore repeats until 20 distinct numbers remain.

modelSteps.text: Use the complete club register and assign the 180 members the distinct labels 001 to 180.
Read successive three-digit groups from the unrestricted random-digit table.
Ignore 000, numbers from 181 to 999, and any number already accepted.
Continue until 20 different valid numbers have been accepted.
Take the 20 members corresponding to those accepted labels.

questions.title: Explain a sampling procedure
questions.context: A school needs 40 students from 197 ordered records. The ratio N/n is 197/40 = 4.925.
questions.task: Explain how you would plan systematic sampling without inventing a universal rounding rule.
questions.focus: Describe the chosen systematic pattern, random starting point and how to ensure 40 selections.
questions.note: Do not claim 'round N/n' automatically works in every case.

extraPoints.text: Check that the systematic pattern actually yields 40 selected units when N/n is non-integer.

modelSteps.text: Number all 197 eligible names in the ordered sampling frame.
Calculate N/n = 197/40 = 4.925, noting that it is not an integer.
Choose a feasible systematic plan. For example, choose a random start of 1 or 2 and then use interval 5.
Select 40 distinct positions, including the start and 39 further positions separated by 5.
Check the final position is at most 197: the final position is 196 when starting at 1 or 197 when starting at 2.

questions.warning: This is one workable scheme, not a universal 'always round N/n' rule. Alternative systematic selection procedures may be defensible if they use a random start and produce the required count.

questions.title: Evaluate a sampling decision
questions.context: A school uses random numbers to choose 30 pupils from a complete register, then concludes the sample must perfectly represent the whole school.
questions.task: Explain why that conclusion is too strong and how to improve the study.

checklist.text: Random selection does not guarantee a representative realised sample.
Even with a complete frame, chance imbalance and nonresponse are possible.
Check response patterns or follow up nonrespondents; acknowledge sampling variation.

questions.model: Using a complete register and a genuine random-number method reduces selection bias, but the realised 30 could be unbalanced by chance. Some pupils may not respond, so I would follow up the chosen pupils and report the limitation.
hints: Identify the population the conclusion is supposed to describe. Which people or items were actually reached?
Could different selections, missing responses or measurement issues change the conclusion?

questions.title: Evaluate a sampling decision

checklist.text: Group targets are fixed in advance.
Individuals within groups are recruited non-randomly, unlike stratified random sampling.
Convenience/nonresponse bias may remain; vary venues and times or use frames for random selection.

questions.model: The interviewer fills two quotas but does not randomly select people within each age group. This is quota sampling, not stratified random sampling. The time and place may bias responses, so recruiting at varied venues or using separate random lists would strengthen the design.
hints: Identify the population the conclusion is supposed to describe. Which people or items were actually reached?

questions.title: Evaluate a sampling decision

Even with a random start, the sample may repeatedly select one cycle position.
Investigate the ordering; simple random selection across the full list or stratification by cycle position may be better.

questions.model: With k = 10, a sample might repeatedly hit the same phase of the ten-item cycle. A random start does not eliminate this risk. I would inspect the ordering and consider simple random selection from the entire numbered list.

questions.task: Explain why increasing the sample to 200 cannot solve the main problem.

Update and verify the frame first, then select distinct units randomly.

questions.model: New members are absent from the list and therefore cannot be chosen at all. A larger sample of old members does not repair this coverage error. I would update the full register and then draw a simple random sample, ignoring repeated random numbers.

questions.title: Evaluate a sampling decision
questions.context: A student wants 40 of 197 ordered names. They divide 197 by 40, round to 5 and claim this is the only correct procedure.
questions.task: Explain what must be checked and why the claim is not justified.

checklist.text: 197/40 is non-integer, so a universal rounding rule is not established.
A defensible systematic rule needs a random start and a selection pattern that produces the intended count.
State and check the chosen procedure rather than assuming one rounded interval works for all cases.

questions.model: Because 197/40 = 4.925, simply rounding to 5 is not a universal sampling rule. I would specify a systematic scheme with a random start, check how many different positions it selects, and make any necessary design adjustment transparently.

questions.title: Evaluate a sampling decision
questions.context: A survey sets proportional age-group quotas but recruits volunteers only from one shopping centre on Saturday afternoon. The authors claim the quotas guarantee the results represent every resident.

Volunteers at one place and time may differ from other residents in each age group.
Use broader recruitment or a suitable frame for stratified random selection and report limitations.

questions.model: Proportional quotas control only the group counts, not how people within those groups are selected. Shopping-centre volunteers may differ from other residents. I would recruit across places and times, or obtain complete age-group frames and randomly draw from each stratum.

questions.title: Identify population and sample
questions.context: A college wants to estimate the mean journey time of all 850 pupils. A questionnaire was given only to 40 members of the cycling club.
questions.task: State the population and the sample, and explain why the result might not represent all pupils.

checklist.text: The population of interest is all 850 pupils, not just cycling club members.
The sample is the 40 cycling-club members who received the questionnaire.
Cyclists may travel differently from other pupils; sample coverage or selection should include the wider school.

questions.model: The population is all 850 pupils, while the sample consists of the 40 cycling-club pupils. Because pupils who cycle might have different journey times from those who travel by bus or car, it would be better to select from a complete list of all eligible pupils.
hints: Define the population and identify the group actually observed before deciding what the result means.

questions.title: A census with missing responses
questions.context: A town council sends a survey to every one of its 500 registered households but only 190 households respond. It calls the 190 replies a complete census of town opinion.
questions.task: Evaluate this claim and describe one limitation.

checklist.text: Inviting the full register is a census attempt, but only 190 households provided observations.
People who did not respond may have different opinions, causing nonresponse bias.
The registered-household list may not include every household, and follow-up or response-rate disclosure is needed.

questions.model: Although the council attempted to collect responses from the whole register, the reported results come from only 190 responding households. The other households may think differently. The council should report its response rate and attempt follow-up, and check whether the register covers the population.
hints: Define the population and identify the group actually observed before deciding what the result means.
Think about sampling variation, who may have been missed and whether the conclusion goes beyond the evidence.

questions.title: Different samples, different estimates
questions.context: Two students each independently take a simple random sample of 30 pupils from the same school. They estimate mean daily screen time as 2.8 hours and 3.5 hours.
questions.task: Explain why the estimates could differ even if both samples were selected correctly.

checklist.text: The two students may select different pupils even when both procedures are genuinely random.
Sample means vary naturally from sample to sample and need not equal the population mean.
Neither sample result alone proves the population mean exactly; describe this uncertainty when drawing a conclusion.

questions.model: The pupils chosen could be different, so the two sample means need not be equal. This is sampling variation, not proof that one student used an incorrect method. Both estimates are uncertain approximations of the school population's mean.
hints: Define the population and identify the group actually observed before deciding what the result means.
Think about sampling variation, who may have been missed and whether the conclusion goes beyond the evidence.

questions.title: When a census may be suitable
questions.context: A small laboratory has 24 reusable measuring devices. The staff can inspect each device in two minutes without damaging it.
questions.task: Choose between a census and sample for checking their calibration. Justify your choice and state a limitation.

checklist.text: A census of all 24 devices is practical because the group is small and inspection is nondestructive.
Checking every device avoids uncertainty caused solely by omitting some devices.
Measurement errors or incorrect calibration procedures are still possible, even with a census.

questions.model: A census is feasible because all 24 devices can be checked in a short time without damage. This means no device is missed merely by sampling, although a poor calibration procedure could still give inaccurate readings.

questions.title: What can this survey tell us?
questions.context: Researchers interview 60 bus passengers at 8 a.m. and report that 70% of all residents travel to work by bus.
questions.task: Critique the inference and suggest a defensible claim or improved sampling method.

checklist.text: Passengers at one bus stop and time do not form a representative selection of all residents.
People who do not work, use other transport or travel later are omitted.
Limit the conclusion to the observed commuters or sample residents through a broader frame/times and locations.

questions.model: The result describes the 60 people interviewed at that time, not necessarily all town residents. Many other residents would never be at this stop. I would use a broader sample of residents or report the result only for those surveyed.
hints: Define the population and identify the group actually observed before deciding what the result means.

questions.title: Two different conclusions
questions.context: Two independent random samples of 50 voters are selected from one complete town register. In one sample a proposed plan has 54% support; in the other it has 46%.
questions.task: Explain how both findings could arise and why neither gives a certain statement about the town.

checklist.text: Independent random samples need not contain the same people.
Sampling variation can yield different sample proportions and even opposite majority results.
Treat the estimates cautiously and avoid claiming the whole town definitely supports or opposes the proposal.

questions.model: Both procedures can be random and valid while selecting different sets of 50 voters. Chance differences can put the estimated support above or below 50%, so neither small sample proves the whole town supports or opposes the plan.
hints: Define the population and identify the group actually observed before deciding what the result means.
Think about sampling variation, who may have been missed and whether the conclusion goes beyond the evidence.

questions.title: A costly national census
questions.context: A business wants the average waiting time of customers across 4,000 stores. It proposes monitoring every transaction for a year, but only has resources to analyse 3,000 transactions.
questions.task: Explain why a sample is reasonable and describe a limitation of the resulting estimate.

checklist.text: Observing all transactions across 4,000 stores for a year would be costly and time-consuming.
A carefully designed sample can reduce workload while giving an estimate of the wider population.
Sampling variability, unequal store coverage and timing may affect conclusions; selection must address these.

questions.model: Monitoring every transaction would be costly, so a manageable sample is reasonable. Selection should cover stores and times appropriately, perhaps with strata. The sample estimate may still differ from the full-population mean due to sampling variation.
hints: Define the population and identify the group actually observed before deciding what the result means.
Think about sampling variation, who may have been missed and whether the conclusion goes beyond the evidence.

questions.title: Nonresponse after random selection
questions.context: An investigator randomly selects 200 employees from a complete staff register. Only 55 reply, mostly people who are enthusiastic about a new workplace policy.
questions.task: Evaluate the claim that the results are unbiased because the original selection was random.

checklist.text: A genuinely random initial selection does not eliminate nonresponse bias.
Those who reply may systematically differ from the 145 who did not.
The researcher should report and investigate the low response rate, follow up selected staff and qualify conclusions.

questions.model: The original selection is random, but only 55 respond; enthusiastic staff may be more likely to reply, biasing the results. I would follow up the selected nonrespondents and explain that the estimate may not represent every employee.
hints: Define the population and identify the group actually observed before deciding what the result means.

questions.title: A small subgroup in the sample
questions.context: Only 8% of a school are boarding pupils. A student takes a simple random sample of 20 pupils and finds no boarding pupils, then concludes there are no boarding pupils at the school.
questions.task: Explain the flaw in the conclusion and propose a better design if boarding pupils must be included.

checklist.text: A random sample can miss a small subgroup by chance, even if the subgroup exists.
Zero boarding pupils in this sample does not show that the full population contains none.
A stratified design can deliberately cover boarding and day pupils, with random selection inside each stratum.

questions.model: There are boarding pupils, but a small random sample can exclude them by chance. This absence is not evidence that no boarding pupils exist. Stratifying by boarding status and randomly choosing within each group would ensure planned coverage.
hints: Define the population and identify the group actually observed before deciding what the result means.

questions.title: A complete-sounding census
questions.context: A survey claims to include every adult in a district, but its register omits newly arrived residents and all residents without internet access.
questions.task: Explain why the census claim is misleading and how the issue could be addressed.

checklist.text: A census requires coverage of the defined population, not merely every record in an incomplete list.
Omitted residents have zero chance of inclusion, so coverage bias remains even if every listed person replies.
The register and contact approach must be improved before making district-wide inferences.

questions.model: The study may survey every person on its list, but that list does not include every adult in the district. The missing groups are systematically excluded. I would update the frame and offer accessible contact routes before interpreting the findings.

questions.title: Generalising from stations

questions.title: Repeated samples are not a contradiction
questions.context: In two independently selected probability samples, 44% and 52% of respondents favour a new timetable. The author calls one result a statistical error because the findings disagree.

checklist.text: Different probability samples can include different respondents.
Both percentages may reflect ordinary sampling variation, especially around a close split.
Examine sample sizes, selection, response and uncertainty instead of declaring one sample automatically incorrect.

The respondents in each group were recruited non-randomly from willing passers-by.
This is quota sampling; stratified random sampling requires random selection within each stratum.

questions.title: When N/n is not an integer

questions.task: Show the numerical problem and an acceptable selection plan.

A defensible allocation such as 41,22,15 or 40,23,15 totals 78; draw randomly within each stratum.
